prime.problem: Five sorts, five complexity claims, and no way yet to know whether someone could do fundamentally better, or which one to actually use. Without the lower bound you can't tell a clever algorithm from an impossible claim.
prime.fits: The comparison card for the whole Sorting part: it needs every sort you've met (insertion through radix) and measures them against one floor, then adds stability as the tie-breaker between sorts that cost the same.
expect: the bound is about the worst input
prime.goal: Prove the n log n floor from the decision tree, spot claims that violate it, and pick the right sort from the when-to-use table.

attend: Why does a binary tree with n! leaves need depth at least log₂ n!?
How can quicksort use 11 compares on a when the floor for n = 7 is 13?
Why does Timsort get within 0.8% of the floor on random input but use only n − 1 compares on sorted input?
Why does sorting by name first and then by team give names in order within each team, and only with a stable sort?
Which assumption would you have to break to go below the floor?

must: A compare-only sort must be able to output each of the n! orders → each compare is one yes/no branch → a tree of depth d has ≤ 2ᵈ leaves → d ≥ log₂ n! ≈ n log₂ n − 1.44n → some input needs that many compares (13 for n = 7; 18,488,885 for 10⁶)

The bound constrains the worst input (and, by average leaf depth, random inputs) → individual inputs can be cheaper (quicksort 11 on a; Timsort n − 1 on sorted data) → adaptivity exploits inputs with far fewer likely orders
Stable sort keeps equal keys in input order → sort by the secondary key, then the primary → ties in the primary keep the secondary order → with an unstable sort use one pass with a tuple key instead
elevated: Same n log n class, different constants: numpy compares raw machine floats, sorted() calls a Python comparison per compare → 0.031 s vs 0.130 s → the bound says nothing about constants
reference: Stirling's formula and the 1.44 = log₂ e constant

compress.prompt: Write the decision-tree argument in three lines of arrows from memory (orders → leaves → depth → compares), then one line on what "stable" buys, then one line on the two ways to beat n log n.
checklist: n! possible input orders, each needs its own leaf
binary tree of depth d has at most 2ᵈ leaves, so d ≥ log₂ n!
log₂ n! ≈ n log₂ n, so Ω(n log n) for any comparison sort
it bounds the worst input, not every input
stable: equal keys keep order, enabling multi-pass multi-key sorts
beat it only by not comparing (radix) or not needing the full order (quickselect, nsmallest)

retrieve.q: Explain why no comparison sort can guarantee fewer than 13 compares on 7 items, without naming any particular algorithm.
answer: 7 items have 7! = 5,040 possible orders; the sort must distinguish them all
each compare splits the remaining possibilities in two at best
2¹² = 4,096 < 5,040, so 12 compares can't separate them; 13 is needed for some input

retrieve.q: Walk through the n = 3 decision tree for insertion sort: which inputs finish after 2 compares, which need 3, and why can't any 3-item sort finish every input in 2?
answer: x y z and y x z finish in 2; the other four orders need 3
a depth-2 tree has at most 4 leaves
3! = 6 orders need 6 leaves, so some path must have depth 3

retrieve.q: You need to sort 10⁶ records by (department, then salary descending) in Python. Two stable passes, or one pass with a tuple key? What does each cost and when does the difference matter?
answer: tuple key: one n log n sort, simplest, works with any sort
two passes: sort by salary, then stably by department; needs a stable sort and costs two sorts
two passes help when keys have mixed directions or can't be combined into one tuple easily; otherwise the tuple key is cheaper

compare.q: Heapsort and merge sort are both Θ(n log n) worst case, yet over all 5,040 orders of a heapsort's worst is 22 compares and merge sort's is 14. What design difference explains it, and does it matter at scale?
answer: merge sort's merges waste few compares (each compare outputs an item); heapsort's sift-downs compare against both children per level
heapsort used ≈ 2.0× the minimum at n = 10⁴ (235,415 vs 118,458)
both stay n log n; the constant factor plus cache behaviour is what shows up in timings

compare.q: Quickselect finds the median in expected O(n), below n log n. Why doesn't that contradict this card?
answer: the bound is for producing the full sorted order (n! outcomes)
the k-th smallest is one of n answers plus a partition, far less information
so it can be found with O(n) compares; the same logic lets heapq.nsmallest run in O(n log k)

predict.q: For n = 4, the floor is ⌈log₂ 24⌉ = 5. Predict the worst case over all 24 orders for bottom-up merge sort and for heapsort (as coded in the card's harness). Which one hits the floor?
predict.answer: Merge sort: 5, exactly the floor. Heapsort: 7. (Insertion sort, Lomuto quicksort and Timsort: 6.) Counted by running the card's Counted wrapper over all 24 permutations. Small n already shows merge sort's economy: each compare outputs one item.

apply.task: Compute the floor ⌈log₂ n!⌉ for n = 4, 8 and 12 (use log₂ n! = Σ log₂ k, or lgamma). Then run the card's compare-counting harness (or reason it through) for merge sort on n = 4 across all 24 orders and confirm it meets the floor.
apply.done: Floors: n = 4 → log₂ 24 = 4.58 → 5; n = 8 → 15.30 → 16; n = 12 → 28.84 → 29. Merge sort's worst over 24 orders of 4 items is 5 compares.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: merge sort hitting the floor, or heapsort's worst case?
Could you explain why the bound is about the worst input, and why that still says something about random inputs?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: n! outcomes → tree depth, or stability → multi-key sorting?
Which row of the when-to-use table would you have got wrong before this card?
What will you watch for in the array-as-hash card: a problem where knowing the value range beats sorting entirely?
